newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi considers BOT for $2 billion power plant.
newsitem.headline: Saudi considers BOT for $2 billion power plant.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's second largest electricity company is considering a build-operate-transfer (BOT) scheme for a $2 billion power plant, part of plans to involve the private sector in state-run utilities.

Bakr Khushaim, director general of the Saudi Consolidated Electricity Company-West (SCECO-West), was quoted by the Saudi daily Arab News on Tuesday as saying local and international firms bidding for the Shuaiba plant project had been asked "to explain how the private sector could contribute towards the construction of the plant under a long-term (BOT agreement)".

"This is the first time that we ask bidders to tell us how private money could contribute in building such plants," Arab News quoted him as saying. "Local capital could be joined by international money in building the plant. We are waiting to see what the competitors (bidders) will offer us."
Khushaim said the utility was seriously considering allowing private investors to build and run the 1,750 megawatt plant for 20 years then transfer it to SCECO-West.
He said bids should be submitted in January and the contract is expected to be awarded a year later.
He did not give an overall cost for the project, but industry experts had told Reuters it was worth $2 billion.
The main part of the contract is for the supply of five 350-megawatt steam turbines, a jetty and a residential compound. SCECO-West is also seeking high-voltage overhead lines.
Shuaiba has been planned since 1993 but delayed by a lack of internal financing.
Saudi Arabia's state-run electricity companies, which charge heavily subsidised, below-cost rates, have been suffering heavy losses amid a tight squeeze on spending by the government.
Electricity demand in the kingdom is close to capacity and official forecasts show demand growing by more than seven percent a year until 2000, mainly from growing industrial demand.
